title: How many cows did the cowherd have?
description: A cowherd's cows pass equally through three gates, then five gates, then seven gates, and there are fewer than two hundred cows. The lowest common multiple of three, five and seven gives the number of cows, and the answer is checked by sharing the cows among the gates.
teaching_notes: One idea: a number that can be shared equally among three, five and seven gates is a common multiple of three, five and seven, and the smallest one below two hundred is the answer. Ask the class to say what kind of number the cows must be before the working is shown. Watch for students who add three, five and seven, or who stop at the first multiple of three.

source: End of chapter Figure it Out, Q5
video_script.why: The child has used the lowest common multiple of two numbers to find when two events happen together and now uses it for three numbers at once.
video_script.substitution: Read each crossing as a multiple, take the lowest common multiple of three, five and seven, and keep the multiple that is below two hundred.
video_script.anchor: Three crossings in a row with three gates, five gates and seven gates, and a herd of cows in front of them.
video_script.payoff_line: The cowherd had one hundred five cows
maths_rules: equal cows through 3 gates: the number is a multiple of 3; likewise of 5 and of 7
3, 5 and 7 share no factor except 1, so LCM = 3 × 5 × 7 = 105
common multiples of 3, 5 and 7: 105, 210, ...; only 105 is below 200
video_script.design: One idea: the number of cows is a common multiple of the gate numbers, and the lowest one below two hundred is the answer. The three crossings stay on the board.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>It comes from the folklore mathematics of Karnataka.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>A cowherd takes all his cows to graze in the fields.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The cows pass a crossing with three gates, and an equal number goes through each gate.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>The same happens at a crossing with five gates, and at one with seven gates.
<bookmark mark='m6'/>He has less than two hundred cows. How many cows does he have?

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>At a crossing, the same number of cows goes through every gate.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>That means the cows can be shared equally among the gates, with none left over.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The smallest number that three, five and seven all go into is called their lowest common multiple.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, the cows go equally through three gates. The number of cows is a multiple of three.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>In the same way, it is a multiple of five and a multiple of seven.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: 3, 5 and 7 share no factor except 1, so LCM = 3 × 5 × 7 = 105

marks.m1: the words common multiple of 3, 5 and 7 are written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, the number is a common multiple of three, five and seven.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Three, five and seven share no factor except one.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The lowest common multiple is three times five times seven, which is one hundred five.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: the next common multiple is 2 × 105 = 210, which is more than 200; so only 105 is below 200

marks.m2: 210 is crossed out as more than 200

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, the next common multiple is two times one hundred five, which is two hundred ten.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>That is more than two hundred, so it is too big. Only one hundred five is below two hundred.

marks.m2: a tick is placed beside each whole number

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, check. One hundred five divided by three is thirty five. Divided by five it is twenty one. Divided by seven it is fifteen.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Every gate gets a whole number of cows, so one hundred five works.
